questions.learningObjective: Identify a reply that is accurate but answers a different claim

options.text: The reply is accurate but answers a different claim from the one the driver made.
The reply is wrong, because the preceding service ran on time that morning.
options.misconception: confuses the fault with a factual error in the reply

options.text: The reply is accurate but the driver made an error in the log entry.
options.misconception: blames the writer rather than the reading of the note

options.text: The reply is accurate and answers the driver's note exactly as written.
options.misconception: misses the mismatch between the reply and the note

questions.explanation: The controller's statement about the preceding service may well be true, but the driver asked about the hold, not its cause. A reply can be entirely accurate and still leave the actual claim untouched.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Requests that a claim be specified
questions.learningObjective: Explain why asking for a claim to be specified sharpens a discussion
questions.stem: A controller asks a driver to explain why the 14:40 was routed around the works. Explain what the controller is asking for and why the phrasing matters.

answer.exemplar: The controller is asking the driver to state the claim, not to justify himself in general terms. Asking why something happened invites a list of circumstances, which can be correct without answering the question of what was claimed about the diversion. Naming the claim to be explained forces both parties onto one proposition, and that is what makes the two accounts comparable rather than merely adjacent.

questions.explanation: Asking for a claim to be specified separates the assertion under dispute from the surrounding circumstances. Vague requests for an explanation let both parties talk past each other.
questions.hint: Ask what the controller wants on the record.

questions.stem: In the log entry above, which standard of proof does the controller apply to the own claim?

options.text: The entry treats the explanation as settled because the controller wrote it down.
options.misconception: confuses recording a statement with establishing it

options.text: The entry proves the claim because no other trains were affected.
options.misconception: treats the absence of contrary evidence as proof

options.text: The entry states the claim as settled but supplies no evidence for it.
The entry applies a higher standard than the driver would need to meet.
options.misconception: assumes the log imposes an elevated evidential standard

questions.explanation: The controller offers no basis for the general claim about the junction, only an assertion. Applying the same evidential standard to one's own claim would require some support beyond the fact of having written it down.
questions.hint: Ask what support is given for the general claim.

questions.learningObjective: Choose the sequence that produces a synthesis rather than a verdict
questions.stem: Two drivers dispute whether a delay was caused by the earlier late arrival or by the platform crowding. Which sequence suits a synthesis discussion of the dispute?

options.text: Let each driver give their account, then vote on which is right.
options.misconception: settles a dispute by majority rather than by synthesis

options.text: Ask the controller to rule, then explain the ruling to the drivers.
options.misconception: confuses deciding the dispute with synthesising it

options.text: Begin with the consequences, then work backwards to the cause.
options.misconception: orders the discussion so the cause is assumed rather than reached

options.text: Set out the shared facts, then locate the step where the accounts diverge.

questions.explanation: A synthesis discussion builds the common ground first, because the disagreement is located in what follows from it. Voting or ruling ends the exchange without producing a position both can use.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What follows from a shared premise
questions.learningObjective: Separate what a shared premise settles from what it leaves open
questions.stem: Two drivers agree that the junction signal was faulty, but one says the delay was unavoidable and the other says it was badly managed. Explain what the shared premise establishes and what it leaves open.

answer.exemplar: The shared premise about the faulty signal establishes that the block was not available as timetabled, which both drivers accept. What follows from it is limited: they disagree about whether a working timetable could have absorbed the failure, and that further step is exactly where their disagreement lies. Naming the shared premise tells them what is no longer in dispute and what still needs arguing.

questions.explanation: A shared premise settles one part of the exchange and leaves the contested step open. Naming it tells the participants what they no longer need to argue about.
questions.hint: Ask what follows and what does not.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A value reply answering a fact complaint

questions.stem: A colleague complains that the 20:10 is always crowded, and another answers that comfort is not what matters on an evening service. Explain how this reply relates to the complaint that was made.

answer.exemplar: The reply offers a value judgement, and it never touches the complaint that the service is always crowded. The two are about different things: one is a claim about what happens on the train, the other about what ought to matter. To be a reply, the value would have to be linked back to the crowding and used to say what would settle the complaint; otherwise the exchange changes subject and the original claim stands unanswered.

questions.explanation: A value judgement answers a factual complaint only when it is linked back to the facts claimed. Here it replaces the complaint with a different subject entirely.
questions.hint: Ask whether the value is tied to the claim.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Standards of proof applied to one's own claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a standard must apply to the writer's own claim
questions.stem: A controller argues in the log that the delay was caused by a late-running service. Explain why the standard applied to that claim should match the one applied to a driver's account.

answer.exemplar: If the controller's own explanation is accepted on the strength of the fact that it was written in the log, then a driver's account can be dismissed on the same basis, and the log becomes a place where assertions are simply recorded. Applying the same evidential requirement to both, which means the explanation has to be supported by something a reader can check, keeps the record usable as evidence rather than as a statement of what the writer believed.

questions.explanation: A standard applied only to other people's claims makes the log a collection of assertions. Applying it to one's own account keeps the record checkable.
questions.hint: Ask what would count as support.

options.text: That the driver who passed it at danger should be asked to explain.

options.text: That the delay was caused by the driver passing at danger.
options.misconception: treats the premise as settling the cause

options.text: That the block was clear when the signal was passed.
options.misconception: infers a fact about the block the premise does not state

options.text: That the circumstances of the passing remain the point in dispute.

questions.explanation: Both drivers accept the fact of the passing, so what remains disputed is the surrounding circumstances and their effect. The agreement fixes one element and leaves the rest of the account open.
questions.hint: Ask what the agreement leaves in dispute.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A reply that is right about the wrong reading
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an accurate but irrelevant reply leaves undone
questions.stem: A driver notes that the 04:15 was cancelled because the rolling stock had no driver. The controller replies that the depot had three spare drivers that evening. Explain what the reply does and does not do.

answer.exemplar: The reply states something that may well be true about the depot, and it addresses a claim the driver never made. The driver recorded that the service lacked a driver, which is a statement about the cancellation, and the reply is about depot staffing levels at a different moment in the evening. As it stands the note stays unaccounted for, and a true statement that does not address the record has done nothing to the exchange.

questions.explanation: The reply is true and still irrelevant to the claim in the note. Accuracy alone does not make a reply an answer.
questions.hint: Ask what the note recorded.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Requests that a claim be specified
questions.learningObjective: Identify the claim left open by a log entry

stimulus.body: Handover request: the incoming driver asks the outgoing driver to explain the delay on the 19:12. The outgoing driver's log records the following line: delay 19:12, held at signal, cause not recorded.

questions.stem: In the handover request above, which reply would specify the claim that needs answering?

options.text: The 19:12 was held at a signal, which the delay record shows.
options.misconception: states a fact without identifying what is being claimed

options.text: Do you claim the hold was caused by the signal rather than by anything else?
The cause has not been recorded, so there is nothing to explain.
options.misconception: treats the absence of a record as the absence of a claim

options.text: You should check the signalling log for that evening.
options.misconception: refers the incoming driver to a source rather than naming the claim

questions.explanation: The log line names an occurrence and leaves the cause blank, so the claim to be specified is what caused the hold. Putting that in question form makes it something the outgoing driver can answer.
questions.hint: Ask what was missing from the log line.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Standards of proof applied to one's own claim
questions.learningObjective: Choose the question that applies the standard to a causal claim
questions.stem: A controller states that the delay was caused by a speed restriction. Which question best applies the evidential standard to that claim?

options.text: Would a driver accept that explanation for a delay of his own?
options.misconception: asks for acceptability rather than for support

options.text: Do speed restrictions usually cause delays of that length?
options.misconception: asks for a generalisation rather than for support in this case

options.text: What in the record shows the restriction was in force at that time?
Has any other driver ever given that explanation before?
options.misconception: asks about precedent rather than about evidence

questions.explanation: The claim needs something in the record that connects the restriction to the delay in question. Asking whether others would accept the explanation, or whether it is common, tests its popularity rather than its support.
questions.hint: Ask what the record would show.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sequence for a synthesis discussion
questions.learningObjective: Select the move that completes a synthesis rather than a ruling
questions.stem: Two drivers dispute the cause of a 21:05 delay. Which final move completes a synthesis rather than a ruling?

options.text: The controller records whichever account has the longer delay list.
options.misconception: settles the dispute by a quantity nobody proposed

options.text: The meeting votes and the majority view is written in the log.
options.misconception: replaces reasoning with a count

options.text: The delay is reclassified under the heading of operational delay.
options.misconception: closes the question by relabelling it rather than resolving it

options.text: Both accounts are recorded along with the evidence that would settle them.

questions.explanation: Recording both accounts and naming the evidence that would resolve the difference produces a position the next person to look at the log can act on. A vote, a majority of delay lists or a relabelling closes the discussion without a synthesis.
questions.hint: Ask what the log must contain afterwards.
